Ask each issuer for a designated withdrawal (or a designated transfer, if the excess came from an RRSP) on Form RC727, for no more than the excess at the time. Do it as early in a month as you can: the current month is taxed either way, and every further month adds 1%.

Ask for a waiver if it was a reasonable error. CRA’s form for this tax is RC729, Request for Waiver or Cancellation of Tax on your Excess FHSA Amount, sent with FHSA statements showing when the excess arose and when it was removed. Penalties and interest go through Form RC4288 instead.

CAD 2,000 designated and withdrawn in October (the default). October is still taxed on its CAD 2,000 high point, and payroll rebuilds CAD 500 and CAD 1,000 in November and December: CAD 65 for 2026. The CAD 1,000 left in December uses part of 2027’s new room, leaving CAD 7,000, and 2027 stays within it.

The 2026 room is entered, not derived. Enter it after any carryforward and re-participation room, within the lifetime limit; the 2027 room is calculated from it with the rules above.

The best single month. Designating the whole excess in July, August, September, October, November or December gives CAD 85, 65, 60, 65, 80 and 105. Early withdrawals are small because the excess is small, and payroll recreates it; late ones come after months of tax. September is the cheapest here, but stopping the payroll contributions in July would beat every one of them.
The excess does not lapse. It carries into the next year as element A and is absorbed only by that year’s new room or by a withdrawal.
The excess uses next year’s room. CRA’s example of a CAD 2,000 excess at the end of 2025 leaves CAD 6,000 of room for 2026, not CAD 8,000.
The lifetime limit still counts the money. Contributions above room count against the CAD 40,000 until they are designated out.

The month of the fix is still taxed. The test is the highest amount at any time in the month, as for a TFSA. Removing the excess on the 28th still leaves that month’s 1%; it stops the tax from the next month. Under the RRSP rule, which uses the month-end, the same withdrawal would avoid the month.

A designated withdrawal is limited to the excess at the time (here $2,000), is not income, and restores that much of the CAD 40,000 lifetime limit. A taxable withdrawal reduces the excess too, but the whole amount is income; any part above the excess becomes re-participation room the next year rather than lifetime room. Waiting lets 1 January absorb the excess, at the cost of months of tax and less new room. Income tax is a flat 30% estimate on the amount, not a return calculation.

A first home savings account (FHSA) has no over-contribution cushion. Any contributions and RRSP transfers above your participation room, across all your FHSAs, are an excess FHSA amount, taxed at 1% of the highest excess at any time in each month. Withdrawing it stops the tax from the next month, not the current one. A designated withdrawal (Form RC727) is tax-free but limited to the excess at that moment, so it cannot get ahead of payroll contributions that are still coming. An excess left at year-end is absorbed by the next January’s room, which leaves less room for that year. In 2024 FHSA holders had 225,210 more accounts than people.

How an FHSA excess starts

If the excess came from an RRSP transfer, a designated transfer back to an RRSP or RRIF is the counterpart of a designated withdrawal; it is not income and does not affect RRSP deduction room. Someone who only contributed can only make a designated withdrawal, and someone who only transferred can only make a designated transfer. The calculator treats contributions and transfers alike and models the withdrawal route.

In 2024, 1.04 million of 1.46 million FHSA holders contributed a total of CAD 6.47 billion, an average of $6,231. In the two highest brackets the average was above CAD 8,000, which is possible only with carried-forward room. Holders had 1,680,490 accounts, 225,210 more than holders; room is shared across all of a person’s FHSAs, which is how many excesses start. Averages are total contributions divided by contributors (CRA rounds counts to 10 and dollars to the thousand); they are not medians. CRA does not publish how many holders had an excess, so this chart shows the people exposed, not the number taxed.

The calculator follows a single person through 2026 and 2027 with a monthly contribution, one lump sum or RRSP transfer, one withdrawal and the new room that arrives on 1 January 2027. It answers four questions: when does the excess start, how much does a withdrawal save and in which month, which kind of withdrawal to use, and how much room is left for next year.

The excess at the end of last year (nil before the first year with an FHSA)
The excess at the time, and no more than your contributions less earlier designated withdrawals

The first home savings account (FHSA) gives each eligible first-time buyer CAD 8,000 of participation room a year, up to CAD 40,000 in a lifetime, with up to CAD 8,000 of unused room carried into the next year. The room belongs to the person, not the account. Most excesses come from that detail: a payroll plan at one institution keeps contributing after a lump sum or an RRSP transfer has gone into an FHSA at another; carried-forward room is counted twice; or a holder assumes that a withdrawal gives room back, as it does for a TFSA the following year.
